look_here_first: SWITCHGRASS — LOOK FIRST AT THE UPPER SURFACE OF A LEAF WHERE IT MEETS THE SHEATH. A conspicuous triangular, often white 'HAIRY ARMPIT' occurs at the blade base; beneath/between the hairs is a SHORT ciliate MEMBRANOUS LIGULE, not Indiangrass's tall pointed 'rifle-sight' membrane. Turn to the seedhead: an expansive AIRY, broad triangular/pyramidal BRANCHED PANICLE with individual small, AWNLESS, typically 3–5 mm spikelets on stalks. Finally examine a many-stemmed warm-season perennial with scaly rhizomes (or compact rhizomatous crown in upland types). Compare true Indiangrass's narrower golden feathery panicle and bent awned spikelets, Johnsongrass's developed spikelet pairs and creeping rhizomes, and the smaller/tufted Panicum hallii. Collar hairs alone do NOT prove switchgrass: look for the combined hairy triangular blade base, shorter ciliolate membrane, panicle structure and awnless spikelets.

project_inclusion.range_basis: Kew/POWO accepts Panicum virgatum and lists Texas in its native range. Hagenbuch & Lemke's Texas Hill Country grass appendix explicitly records Hays County (Bierner 90-208, TEX-LL). The same appendix explicitly records Blanco County (Breckenridge 559, SWT). The same appendix explicitly records Val Verde County (Smith & Butterwick 202, TEX-LL). Kerr County: Singhurst et al. 2010 Kerr WMA flora, published vouchers JS 9985, FG 8470, LS 3927. Valid target counties Hays, Blanco, Kerr; former Val Verde is out of zone.

best_field_traits: Perennial warm-season tall grass, often 1–2 m or taller at flowering, caespitose with scaly rhizomes (upland plants can have short rhizomes).

Leaf blade base has a dense, often TRIANGULAR patch of long white/silky hairs when exposed at the collar; a small membranous ligule with a fringed edge is beneath the hairs (the patch is NOT a true auricle).
Broad, open, spreading pyramidal panicle, usually 15–55 cm, with many fine ascending/spreading branches.
Individual spikelets typically 3–5 mm, borne singly on slender pedicels; awnless, unlike Sorghastrum nutans.
Leaves often broad, flat and relatively smooth away from the blade-base tuft; midrib typically evident; leaf blade color is highly variable.
Observe true basal rhizomes for distinction from annual Panicum capillare and tufted P. coloratum, but don't force a sterile specimen by rhizome length.
morphology_keys.joey_family_training: Use the completed Poaceae morphology framework: inflorescence architecture first, then spikelets, glumes, lemma/palea, awns, ligule, collar, sheath and nodes.

comparisons.key_distinctions: FIRST expose the triangular HAIR PATCH at the upper leaf blade base and the much shorter ciliate membrane (no stiff rifle-sight projection). NEXT trace the broad AIRY panicle and separate single unawned small spikelets. Indiangrass has a taller notched membranous collar, narrower tawny panicle and BENT AWNS; Johnsongrass has a large open panicle too but fertile sessile/pedicelled pairs and robust rhizomes, lacking the distinctive triangular hair patch. Hall's panicgrass is generally smaller and bluer with basal leaves and shorter stiffly branching panicle; witchgrass is a hairy annual with an extremely diffuse irregular panicle; kleingrass is an introduced tufted perennial with a knotty crown. No cultivar IDs from leaf color.

not_reliable_alone: Open airy panicle: Johnsongrass, witchgrass and some other Panicums can look similar.
Tall stand or stiff large blades: several prairie grasses overlap.
Hairy collar in isolation: other grasses have hair-fringed ligules.
Red-purple or blue foliage: variable and often selected in cultivars, not a local wild-type ID.
A rhizomatous base alone: Johnsongrass and other perennial grasses are rhizomatous.

photo_diagnostic_lesson.title: Switchgrass: hairy armpit → airy panicle → awnless spikelet

steps.look: TRIANGULAR tuft of white hairs at the upper blade base
steps.what: At the blade–sheath junction spread a mature leaf outward, photograph the hair patch on the TOP surface near the blade base. Some look cup-shaped or less triangular; inspect several leaves. Distinguish these hairs from general sheath fuzz.

steps.look: Short membranous edge fringed with hairs, usually hidden in tufts
steps.what: Do not describe the white hairs as a stiff triangle-shaped membrane. Compare Indiangrass's prominent two-pointed rifle-sight ligule.

steps.look: One broad, airy, many-branched terminal panicle
steps.what: Trace fine panicle branches to individual slender pedicels. Indiangrass is usually narrower/denser with awns; big bluestem has turkey-foot racemes.

steps.look: Single AWNLESS, oval ~3–5 mm spikelet, not a pair of fertile and pedicelled units
steps.what: Use 5–10× lens on mature spikelet. Contrast Indiangrass's bent twisted awn and Johnsongrass's spikelet pairing; do not confuse panicle stalk for awn.

steps.look: Perennial many-stemmed crown with scaly rhizomes
steps.what: On an appropriate specimen expose rhizome segments at soil level. Some upland ecotypes have short rhizomes; do not claim non-native based on rhizome length.

photo_diagnostic_lesson.memory_rule: SWITCHGRASS = HAIRY TRIANGLE at blade base + AIRY PANICLE + AWNLESS single spikelets.

diagnostic_second_pass_20261022.status: FIELD_READY_PHOTO_GAPS — high-coverage anatomy, not formally FINISHED
crew_teaching_sequence: 1. Find the entire robust perennial stand, then trace its underground spreading stem. The sl25 original photographed stem base with actual scaly RHIZOME; habitat photo alone is not species proof.

2. At attached blade–sheath junction look for compact white silky HAIR TRIANGLE. On sl37 three existing audited markers identify two true hair tufts and a 5mm scale. True thin underlying membrane remains partly hidden.

NEW: between the intact sl37 white silky hair photo and panicle, show Bob Harms actual opened PAVI2-L collar/sheath composite with original scale. An intact hair triangle is NOT equivalent to proving the tiny MEMBRANOUS ligule; inspect exposed cut sections and separate real membrane edge from sheath and collateral hairs; do not place an unverified arrow or infer length.
3. Follow actual culm to a complete broadly pyramidal OPEN PANICLE — sl33. Don't confuse an isolated tiny flowering branch with the WHOLE flowering head.
4. At sl40 actual 5mm source reference select ONE truly AWNLESS Panicum spikelet with its fine pedicel; purple feathery units are STIGMAS, not Indiangrass-type awns.
5. Study sl53 REAL labeled PHOTO montage: Glu refers to GLUMES outside and Lem to LEMMAS, Pal to PALEAS of lower sterile/staminate and upper fertile florets; count the florets within ONE spikelet.
6. Match sl55 TRUE upper fertile flower enclosed by hardened lemma and palea, then the original stored ripe seed photo. The grain is not the whole spikelet.

7. Compare DIFFERENT species Sorghastrum nutans actual rifle-sight collar/awns and Paspalum floridanum tall clump, few one-sided spikelet-bearing racemes; the Paspalum comparison does not illustrate its membrane.

8. Record confirmation: real local matched rhizome, exact short ciliate membrane edge, ripe glumes/lemma/palea at mm scale. If any are unresolved use Panicum cf. virgatum for hard IDs, no unearned FINISHED.

items.caption: DIFFERENT SPECIES — Florida paspalum. A similarly robust grass clump can resemble switchgrass if neither is blooming. Florida paspalum's true flowering racemes and larger paired flattened one-sided spikelets are decisive; its brown membranous ligule requires a separate actual collar photo. This broad clump picture does NOT demonstrate that membrane.
items.why_it_matters: Avoid diagnosing switchgrass from a tall green stand or general blade width; trace the actual flowering architecture and collar.

visual_comparison.memory_rule: MEMBRANE != WHITE HAIRS: true Panicum virgatum ligule consists of a short ciliate membrane with longer white silky hairs around/behind it; membrane can weather off on older leaves. Open the leaf sheath gently to locate it, and compare Harms dissected plate with the actual sl37 hair photograph.

field_photo_quickcheck.heading: Switchgrass: hairy triangle, airy plume, awnless seeds
steps: FIRST inspect the locally archived switchgrass stand, then the licensed external photographer-labelled attached rhizome. The latter is not yet physically archived or a local Texas plant voucher.

SECOND use Stefan.lefnaer's archived collar macro for the white silky blade-base hair triangle, then Bob Harms' separately archived opened ligule/sheath with source scale. The hair triangle is visible; do not guess the tiny membrane TIP position from the unannotated dissection.
THIRD examine the actual broadly branched open panicle (Stefan.lefnaer external whole-head view), followed by the archived side branch with attached awnless spikelets and exserted feathery stigmas.

FOURTH use Stefan.lefnaer's externally hosted original-author-labelled spikelet dissection to distinguish glumes, lower/upper lemmas and palea, followed by the fertile-floret close-up. These are not locally archived or independently arrow-certified.

LAST compare the true collar with the DIFFERENT SPECIES Indiangrass rifle-sight ligule; same-specimen local rhizome, collar membrane tip and mature measured spikelet images are needed before a 100% claim.
field_photo_quickcheck.field_rule: SWITCHGRASS = HAIRY TRIANGLE at blade base + AIRY PANICLE + AWNLESS single spikelets.
